core: Observation, inference, evaluation, and contextual claims
Flexible use of musical elements and listening context
supporting: Rhythm, pitch, timbre, texture, dynamics, form, performers, and production
A method for concise evidence-based paragraphs
outOfScope: Detailed genre history or repertory surveys
Exact instrument or production identification from sound alone
Claims about medical effects, creator intent, or cultural function without sources

claims.claim: Music unfolds through time, so listening can track earlier sounds, later expectations, repetition, contrast, return, and change.
Pitch, dynamics or volume, articulation, timbre, melody, harmony, rhythm, texture, and form are useful introductory vocabulary for describing sound.
A sound-focused claim can distinguish time-located observation from inference, evaluation, and contextual claim, each of which requires a different kind of support.
Recorded and live contexts offer different listening evidence, including replayability, production layers, performers, space, and audience conditions.
Composer, performer, and producer are distinct roles that may overlap, and producer decisions can shape the overall sound of a recording.
Recording processes can layer separately made tracks and mix them into a finished sound, so a listener should not infer an exact live setup solely from a recording.
A responsible analyst can use repeat listening and time-stamped observations to form qualified interpretations without forcing every excerpt into a standard genre, meter, key, or form.
